title: A Multi-Stage Optimized Framework for Fundus Image Classification in Diabetic Retinopathy
abstract: Abstract Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a progressive retinal disease and is a major contributor to irreversible blindness in diabetic patients globally. Recognizing retinal lesions early and correctly will be vital to preventing vision impairment and for timely clinical intervention. This study introduces an intelligent optimization-based framework for automated detection of diabetic retinopathy, where Improved Grey Wolf Optimization (IGWO) is used to preprocess the retinal images, Improved Whale Optimization Algorithm (IWOA) to segment lesions in the retinal images, Improved Artificial Bee Colony (IABC) to select features from the retinal images, and an Improved Fuzzy Support Vector Machine (IFSVM) to detect the diabetic retina. First, the images of the retina undergo enhancement for image contrast, reduction of noise and illumination variations with IGWO. The improved images are then segmented applying IWOA for precise estimation of the lesion regions. The image segments of the lesions are then used to extract comprehensive colour, texture and shape features, which are then optimized using IABC to remove redundant information while retaining highly discriminative features. Lastly, the optimized feature subset is classified by using the proposed IFSVM. The preprocessing stage of IGWO had a PSNR of 38.64 dB, SSIM of 0.986, MSE of 0.0042, entropy of 7.82, contrast improvement index of 2.06 and processing time of 0.78 s. The IWOA segmentation algorithm proposed in this paper achieved a Dice coefficient of 98.42%, IoU of 96.89%, sensitivity of 98.51%, specificity of 98.83%, precision of 98.46%, and overall segmentation accuracy of 98.68%. The IABC algorithm has only 82 informative features (with a feature reduction of 65.6%), and only 6.41s to optimize. The proposed Improved Fuzzy Support Vector Machine demonstrated superior classification accuracy (98.55%), precision (98.48%), recall (98.51%), F1-score (98.49%) and AUC (99.02%) compared to the rest of the conventional machine learning and deep learning methods. The robust performance of the proposed framework was also statistically validated by 5-fold cross validation with a mean accuracy of 98.55% with a standard deviation of 0.13% which resulted in statistically significant p-values less than 0.005 and narrow confidence intervals.

title: Relapsing Multiple Cranial Neuropathies as a Manifestation of Neurosyphilis: A Case Report and Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Neurosyphilis is an infectious disease of the central nervous system caused by Treponema pallidum. Its incidence has been increasing globally. Due to variable clinical presentations, nonspecific symptoms, and diverse latency periods, neurosyphilis is frequently misdiagnosed or missed altogether. It commonly involves a single cranial nerve.We report a rare case of neurosyphilis presenting with multiple cranial nerve involvement as the initial manifestation. The patient was admitted with progressive cranial neuropathies. Comprehensive evaluations, including serologic tests, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis, and cranial MRI, were conducted. Laboratory findings supported the diagnosis of neurosyphilis, with positive serum and CSF Treponema pallidum antibodies, CSF pleocytosis, and elevated protein levels. MRI revealed abnormal enhancement of multiple cranial nerves. The patient was treated with high-dose intravenous penicillin, resulting in gradual clinical improvement.This case highlights the diagnostic challenges posed by atypical neurosyphilis presentations. By reviewing this rare case and relevant literature, we aim to improve clinicians' awareness of neurosyphilis with polycranial neuritis and promote timely diagnosis and effective treatment.

title: Changes in tumor volume predict overall survival after [177Lu]Lu-DOTATATE in neuroendocrine neoplasm
abstract: Abstract Purpose Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) is a crucial therapy for neuroendocrine neoplasms (NENs). Pre-treatment somatostatin receptor (SSTR) PET determines eligibility for PRRT and can prognosticate overall survival (OS). The prognostic value of an end-of-treatment (EOT) SSTR-PET is underexplored. Methods 132 NEN patients who were treated with PRRT and underwent baseline and EOT SSTR-PET/CTs were retrospectively identified. Tumor lesions were semi-automatically annotated and total tumor volume (TTV), SUV max and SUV mean were derived from both PET scans and relative change in PET parameters were calculated. Associations between PET parameters and OS were assessed with Cox regression and Kaplan-Meier analyses. Results Higher baseline TTV and increased TTV at EOT were significantly associated with shorter OS, while baseline and EOT SUV metrics were not independently associated with OS. Conclusion Increased TTV at baseline and EOT SSTR-PET/CT portends shorter OS in NEN and may guide clinical decision-making.

title: Radioclinical Characteristics, Diagnostic Approaches, and Clinical Outcomes of Abdominal Tuberculosis: A Six-Year Retrospective Study from a Tertiary Hospital in Somalia
abstract: Abstract Background Abdominal tuberculosis (ATB) is one of the most challenging forms of extrapulmonary tuberculosis because of its nonspecific clinical presentation and radiological resemblance to gastrointestinal malignancies and inflammatory bowel diseases. We conducted a Six-year retrospective observational study to evaluate the radioclinical characteristics, diagnostic approaches, and clinical outcomes of patients with abdominal tuberculosis at a tertiary referral hospital in Somalia. Methods This retrospective study included 286 patients diagnosed with abdominal tuberculosis between January 2019 and December 2024. Patients were classified as confirmed ATB when diagnosis was established by histopathology, microbiological culture, GeneXpert MTB/RIF, or a combination of these methods, and as presumed ATB when diagnosis was based on compatible clinical presentation, characteristic radiological findings after exclusion of alternative diagnoses. Demographic characteristics, clinical manifestations, computed tomography (CT) findings, diagnostic procedures, treatment strategies, and clinical outcomes were analyzed using SPSS version 26. Associations between categorical variables were assessed using Pearson's chi-square test, with P < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Results Among the 286 patients, 226 (79.0%) had confirmed abdominal tuberculosis, while 60 (21.0%) were classified as presumed cases. The majority were young adults, with the highest proportion belonging to the 20–39-year age group. Multiple-site abdominal involvement was the predominant radiological pattern (236/286, 82.5%), followed by isolated peritoneal tuberculosis (47/286, 16.4%). Paracentesis was the most frequently performed diagnostic procedure (186/286, 65.0%). Initial radiological assessment correctly identified abdominal tuberculosis in 243 patients (85.0%), whereas 43 patients (15.0%) were initially misdiagnosed, including 39 (13.6%) as malignancy, and 4 (1.4%) as Crohn's disease, before microbiology-pathological confirmation. Most patients improved following anti-tuberculosis therapy (233/286, 81.5%), while 39 (13.6%) died and 14 (4.9%) were lost to follow-up. Prolonged symptom duration was significantly associated with the need for surgical intervention (P < 0.05). Conclusions Abdominal tuberculosis remains a major diagnostic challenge in tuberculosis-endemic, resource-limited settings because of its nonspecific clinical and radiological features. An integrated diagnostic approach combining clinical assessment, contrast-enhanced CT, histopathological examination, microbiological testing, and molecular diagnostics is essential for improving diagnostic accuracy and reducing unnecessary surgical intervention. These findings provide important evidence to strengthen the diagnosis and management of abdominal tuberculosis in Somalia and other high-burden settings.

title: New-Onset Continuous Urinary Incontinence After Ectopic Ureteral Stone Surgery with Pre-existing Stress Urinary Incontinence: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Adult ectopic ureter is uncommon and may be overlooked when a common cause of urinary incontinence coexists. Case presentation: A 66-year-old woman had a 2-year history of intermittent urinary leakage during coughing or physical activity. She later developed right flank pain and fever. Computed tomography (CT) demonstrated bilateral duplicated collecting systems and a right upper-pole ectopic ureter opening into the urethra, with an approximately 11×8 mm calculus impacted near its distal opening (Fig. 1A, B). Ureteroscopic lithotripsy relieved the flank pain. Subsequent urodynamic evaluation demonstrated moderate stress urinary incontinence (SUI) (Fig. 1C), and a tension-free vaginal tape (TVT) procedure initially improved the leakage. One month after TVT, however, the leakage changed to continuous urine loss unrelated to coughing, activity, or body position. Repeat urodynamics were normal, and the leaking fluid remained clear during bladder methylene blue instillation. Cystoscopic reassessment and review of the known duplicated anatomy raised suspicion of an ectopic urinary source (Fig. 2A). Laparoscopy confirmed the ectopic right upper-pole ureter (Fig. 2B), which was reimplanted into the bladder. Postoperative retrograde pyelography documented the reconstructed system (Fig. 2C), and the patient no longer experienced urinary leakage. Conclusion: This case illustrates that ectopic ureter may be easily missed when coexisting SUI provides a convincing explanation for urinary leakage. A transition from stress-related intermittent leakage to continuous, position-independent leakage should trigger reassessment of the diagnosis. In patients with a duplicated collecting system, integration of symptom phenotype, urodynamics, dye testing, cystoscopy, and cross-sectional imaging can help identify an ectopic urinary source and avoid diagnostic delay.

title: Deco-CLIP: Dual-Branch Feature Decoupling CLIP for Fine-Grained Zero-Shot Medical Image Analysis
abstract: Abstract The CLIP model has been widely used in the medical field, improving the efficiency of disease screening and diagnosis by establishing feature-level associations between medical images and radiology reports. However, we have found that the contrastive learning strategy of current medical CLIP primarily focuses on distinguishing high-level semantic features. Therefore, it fails to capture the low-level features related to attributes and relational information, limiting performance in fine-grained tasks. To address these limitations, we propose Deco-CLIP to decouple representational features from semantic features. Specifically, the image modality consists of two Vision Transformer (ViT) encoders that extract semantic and texture features using different pretraining strategies. The text modality consists of a text encoder with dual branches to focus on tokens representing high- and low-level features. Furthermore, to enhance the model's ability to capture fine-grained features, we propose a threshold-adaptive sample mining strategy based on intra-modal similarity, which clusters semantically similar samples into mini-batches. Then, secondary contrastive learning is applied within the mini-batch to align the fine-grained features between image and text modalities. Additionally, a regularized attention mechanism is proposed to guide the two branches of the text encoder to focus on distinct feature representations. We evaluated Deco-CLIP on fine-grained zero-shot tasks, including multi-abnormality detection and report-to-volume retrieval. The results showed a 10.2\% improvement in accuracy for multi-abnormality detection and a 16.2\% increase in recall for report-to-volume retrieval, demonstrating the effectiveness of Deco-CLIP in fine-grained medical tasks. The code will be publicly released.

title: Intralymphatic Blood Flow in Secondary Lymphedema: A Novel Finding and Its Clinical Implications – A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Intact lymphatic vessels maintain strict blood-lymphatic segregation. While pathological blood-lymphatic mixing occurs in genetic animal models, spontaneous intralymphatic blood filling has not been clinically documented. Methods A 55-year-old woman with secondary upper-extremity lymphedema following mastectomy presented with abnormal blood flow signals within lymphatic lumina on preoperative high-frequency ultrasound. She had chronic aspirin use and developed acute severe hypertension (220/100 mmHg) with extensive cutaneous ecchymosis preoperatively. Six lymphaticovenous anastomoses were performed under microscopy. Results Intraoperative visualization confirmed blood-filled lymphatic vessels, corroborating ultrasound findings. At 3-month follow-up, the corrected edema reduction rate reached 33.68%, with clinically meaningful improvements in body image, symptom, and mood subdomains of the LYMQOL-Arm scale. Conclusions This represents the first clinical evidence of intralymphatic blood filling. We hypothesize acute hypertension exacerbated venous reflux through latent lymphovenous communications, while aspirin disrupted physiological platelet-mediated blood-lymphatic segregation. LVA remains feasible when intraoperative assessment confirms higher intralymphatic pressure and favorable flow directionality, though single-case limitations apply.

title: Pulmonary non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease masquerading as recurrent tuberculosis in Nigeria: diagnostic complexities and therapeutic challenges from a 17-year longitudinal case report
abstract: Abstract Background Pulmonary non-tuberculous mycobacterial disease (NTM-LD) is increasingly recognised as an important cause of chronic pulmonary infection worldwide. However, in tuberculosis (TB)-endemic settings, NTM-LD remains underdiagnosed because clinical algorithms and laboratory services are primarily designed to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Consequently, patients are frequently misdiagnosed, receive repeated empirical anti-tuberculosis treatment, and experience delays in appropriate management. Case presentation We report a 17-year longitudinal case of an immunocompetent Nigerian man whose chronic respiratory illness ultimately proved to be pulmonary NTM disease. The patient had previously completed treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis in 2004 and presented to the University of Port Harcourt Teaching Hospital in 2009 with chronic productive cough, low-grade fever, weight loss, drenching night sweats, and exertional dyspnoea. Chest radiography demonstrated extensive unilateral fibrocavitary lung disease, while three sputum specimens were negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Based on his clinical history and prevailing national tuberculosis treatment guidelines, he was empirically treated for relapsed pulmonary tuberculosis with a Category II anti-tuberculosis regimen. Despite modest clinical improvement, persistent symptoms and progressive radiographic destruction of the left lung prompted further evaluation. Repeat sputum microscopy detected AFB in one of two specimens, raising suspicion of drug-resistant tuberculosis. Mycobacterial culture performed at the Nigerian Institute of Medical Research yielded a non-tuberculous mycobacterium. Subsequent molecular testing confirmed that the isolate was not a member of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex; however, species identification and drug susceptibility testing were unavailable due to diagnostic limitations. Given the extensive cavitary lung disease, chronic pulmonary aspergillosis was also considered, and empirical itraconazole therapy was initiated while further investigations were pursued. The patient subsequently received rifampicin- and clarithromycin-based therapy with gradual clinical improvement. However, irreversible structural lung damage resulted in destroyed left lung syndrome and chronic bronchiectasis requiring long-term respiratory follow-up. Conclusions This case highlights the substantial diagnostic and therapeutic challenges of pulmonary NTM disease in resource-limited, TB-endemic settings. It demonstrates the limitations of relying on AFB microscopy and empirical TB treatment, the importance of recognizing discordant microbiological findings, and the consequences of limited access to mycobacterial species identification and drug susceptibility testing. Strengthening laboratory capacity, integrating NTM into national TB diagnostic algorithms, and improving clinician awareness are essential for facilitating timely diagnosis and appropriate management.

title: Clinical analysis of mycosis fungoides involving the central nervous system：a case report
abstract: Abstract Background Mycosis fungoides (MF) with central nervous system (CNS) involvement is a rare complication of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma(CTCL) without unified diagnostic and therapeutic criteria.We retrospectively analyzed the clinical presentation, diagnostic and therapeutic course, and prognosis of a single case of MF with CNS involvement treated at our institution.Combined neuroimaging, cerebrospinal fluid flow cytometry suggested CNS infiltration, and stereotactic biopsy, histopathology together with positive T-cell receptor gene rearrangement confirmed the diagnosis.This case indicates high vigilance for CNS dissemination in MF patients with new neurological symptoms. It highlights that CNS involvement should be suspected in MF patients with new neurological symptoms, and combined imaging, cerebrospinal fluid testing and biopsy enables timely diagnosis of CNS dissemination in advanced MF. Case Presentation: We report a 49-year-old male with mycosis fungoides (MF) who developed new-onset left facial hypesthesia and left upper limb weakness. Neuroimaging revealed a right frontal lobe lesion with multiple extracranial hypermetabolic foci. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed aberrant T-lymphocytes, supporting a diagnosis of MF with central nervous system (CNS) involvement. The patient initially responded to systemic chemotherapy but was subsequently complicated by septic shock and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Two months later, follow-up imaging showed new brain lesions; stereotactic biopsy and positive T-cell receptor gene rearrangement confirmed persistent CNS involvement. Conclusions This case highlights that in MF patients presenting with CNS symptoms,the diagnosis of MF with CNS involvement should be considered and an aggressive diagnostic workup, including imageological assessment, lumbar puncture, tissue biopsy and so on, should be pursued to establish a diagnosis. Therapeutic strategies must be individualized based on each patient's specific disease status.

title: Delayed Diagnosis of Kartagener Syndrome in an Adolescent with Recurrent Sinopulmonary Infections and Severe Bronchiectasis: The First Reported Case from Somalia
abstract: Abstract Background Kartagener syndrome is a rare form of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by chronic sinopulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, and situs inversus. Diagnosis is frequently delayed because respiratory manifestations are nonspecific and specialized diagnostic testing may be unavailable, particularly in resource-limited settings. We report what is, to our knowledge, the first reported case of Kartagener syndrome from Somalia, highlighting the diagnostic and management challenges encountered in a resource-limited setting. Case presentation A 15-year-old girl from rural Somalia presented with a lifelong history of recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic productive cough, progressive exertional dyspnea, and intermittent hemoptysis. Examination revealed digital clubbing and signs of chronic respiratory disease. Chest radiography and contrast-enhanced computed tomography demonstrated dextrocardia, situs inversus totalis, and extensive bilateral cystic bronchiectasis with superimposed bronchopneumonia. A clinical diagnosis of Kartagener syndrome was made based on the characteristic phenotype, radiological findings, and a PICADAR score of 8/14. Confirmatory investigations, including ciliary function studies and genetic testing, were unavailable because of resource limitations. Family education focused on airway-clearance techniques, recognition of respiratory exacerbations, treatment adherence, and long-term follow-up. Because of the substantial geographic distance from specialist care, follow-up was coordinated with a local primary care physician and supported by telemedicine. At 1 month, her cough and sputum production had markedly decreased, respiratory distress had resolved, and she had returned to school and daily activities. Conclusions Kartagener syndrome should be considered in children and adolescents with recurrent sinopulmonary infections, chronic rhinosinusitis, bronchiectasis, and laterality abnormalities. In resource-limited settings, characteristic clinical and radiological findings can facilitate recognition when definitive diagnostic testing is unavailable, although the limitations of a clinical diagnosis should be acknowledged. Early recognition, sustained airway-clearance therapy, appropriate treatment of respiratory infections, and patient- and family-centered education are important for long-term disease management. This case also illustrates how locally coordinated and remote follow-up may help maintain continuity of care when access to specialized respiratory services is limited.

title: Oral Foregut Duplicate cyst presenting as tongue-tie in a pediatric patient: a clinicopathologic case report
abstract: Abstract Oral foregut duplication cysts (OFDCs) are rare congenital anomalies arising from abnormal foregut development during embryogenesis, characterized by ectopic gastrointestinal or respiratory epithelium within the oral cavity. We present the case of a 6-year-old boy referred to with a presumptive diagnosis of ankyloglossia ("tongue-tie") who was found to have a well-circumscribed midline cystic mass within the intrinsic muscles of the tongue. MRI demonstrated a homogeneous T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense lesion with increased diffusivity and minimal wall enhancement. The mass was excised via a ventral tongue approach and delivered intact. Histopathologic examination revealed a cyst wall lined by ciliated respiratory-type epithelium with an underlying smooth muscular layer, consistent with an oral foregut duplication cyst. The differential diagnosis, including ranula, leiomyoma, rhabdomyoma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, is discussed. This case highlights the importance of considering foregut duplication cysts in the differential diagnosis of congenital tongue masses, particularly when clinical presentation mimics ankyloglossia. Complete surgical excision is curative, with a low risk of recurrence.

title: Application Effects of Modified Coronectomy in Mandibular Third Molars with High-Risk Proximity to the Mandibular Canal and Characteristics of Residual Root Migration
abstract: Abstract Objective To evaluate the perioperative outcomes, the protective effect on the inferior alveolar nerve, and the migration characteristics of residual roots within 12 months postoperatively following a modified coronectomy in cases of high-risk contact between the mandibular third molar root and the mandibular canal. Materials and Methods The study included 73 patients treated at the Department of Stomatology, First Affiliated Hospital of the Army Medical University, from November 2023 to July 2025. All patients underwent preoperative cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) scans and were divided into three groups based on the surgical procedure performed: the exodontia group (33 patients), the coronectomy group (5 patients), and the modified coronectomy group (35 patients). The primary outcome was postoperative sensation in the lower lip and chin, secondary outcomes included operative time, intraoperative blood loss, postoperative pain, facial swelling, limited mouth opening, temporomandibular joint clicking, and residual root migration. Clinical and radiographic follow-up lasted up to 12 months. Results The operative time in the modified coronectomy group was 51.30 ± 19.63 min, which was longer than the 32.97 ± 13.81 min in the exodontia group (P < 0.001); intraoperative blood loss was 15.07 ± 7.03 mL and 10.42 ± 5.88 mL, respectively (P < 0.05); Visual Analog Scale (VAS) scores on postoperative day 3 were 2.50 ± 0.75 and 3.09 ± 1.35, respectively (P < 0.05). No inferior alveolar nerve injury was observed in the modified coronectomy group, whereas the incidence in the exodontia group was 12.12% (P < 0.001); associated sensory abnormalities resolved approximately 3 months postoperatively. Residual root displacement increased with extended follow-up. At 12 months postoperatively, the migration distances for the groups with residual root lengths of ≤ 5 mm, 5–10 mm, and > 10 mm were 4.82 ± 0.59 mm, 3.06 ± 0.81 mm, and 4.13 ± 0.75 mm. After stratification by root morphology, the fusion root group exhibited more pronounced migration in the later stages, while the single-root group showed the lowest migration at 12 months. Conclusion In this study, no inferior alveolar nerve injury was observed in the modified coronectomy group, and postoperative pain scores were low. However, this procedure involved a longer operative time and relatively higher intraoperative blood loss. Residual root migration may be related to residual root length and root morphology, with 5–10 mm residual roots exhibiting relatively better stability during the 12-month follow-up period. Clinical Implications: For mandibular third molars where the root is closely associated with the mandibular canal and complete extraction may increase the risk of inferior alveolar nerve injury, modified coronectomy can serve as an alternative treatment strategy. During surgery, attention should be paid to the complete removal of enamel, control of residual root length, and preservation of alveolar bone, and standardized postoperative follow-up should be implemented.

title: Orbital Complications Following Acute Rhinosinusitis in Children: Clinical Outcomes Across Chandler Classification Stages
abstract: Abstract Purpose Periorbital and orbital cellulitis represent a spectrum of paediatric infections associated with potentially serious complications. Although widely used, the Chandler classification has limited evidence supporting its role in predicting disease severity and guiding management in children. This study evaluated the clinical utility of the Chandler classification and explored a preliminary risk stratification model for severe disease. Methods This retrospective observational cohort study included patients aged under 18 years admitted with periorbital or orbital cellulitis between January 2023 and December 2025. Patients were classified according to Chandler stages I–IV. Demographic, clinical, microbiological, radiological and outcome data were extracted from electronic records. Pearson’s chi-square tests and ordinal logistic regression were used to identify associations and independent predictors of severe disease. Results Eighty-six patients were included: 87.2% had Chandler stage I disease, 2.3% stage II, 5.8% stage III and 4.7% stage IV. Time from presentation to CT imaging demonstrated the strongest association with Chandler stage (χ² = 90.78, p < 0.001), followed by surgical management, nasal steroid use and sinus involvement. Ophthalmoplegia and proptosis were strongly associated with advanced disease. In dichotomised analyses comparing mild (stages I–II) and severe disease (stages III–IV), time to CT imaging showed the largest effect size. Exploratory regression analyses identified admission duration as independently associated with increasing Chandler stage, while age and admission duration were independently associated with severe disease in the dichotomised analysis. Conclusions The Chandler classification differentiates disease severity in paediatric orbital infections and may support early recognition of patients requiring escalated care.

title: Deficient Mismatch Repair, Mucinous Histology, and Systemic Inflammation Are Associated with Nodal Overstaging on Preoperative Computed Tomography in Right-Sided Colon Cancer: A Propensity Score–Matched Study
abstract: Abstract Background Accurate preoperative nodal staging is increasingly important as neoadjuvant immunotherapy emerges for mismatch repair-deficient (dMMR) colon cancer. CT-based N-overstaging may be more frequent in dMMR than in mismatch repair-proficient (pMMR) tumors; however, because dMMR status, mucinous histology, and systemic inflammation often coexist in right-sided colon cancer, we assessed their associations with nodal misclassification. Methods We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent resection for right-sided colon adenocarcinoma. Patients with dMMR tumors were propensity score–matched to those with pMMR tumors based on age and sex, with exact matching on pT, pN, and mucinous histology. Clinicopathological, molecular, and inflammation-related factors were evaluated using logistic regression. Results The matched cohort comprised 80 dMMR and 78 pMMR patients. Among 106 pathologically node-negative patients, N-overstaging occurred in 29 (53.7%) dMMR and 19 (36.5%) pMMR tumors ( P = 0.076). After multivariable adjustment, dMMR status (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 2.49; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.02–6.11; P = 0.046), mucinous histology (aOR, 4.65; 95% CI, 1.02–21.24; P = 0.047), and modified Glasgow Prognostic Score (mGPS) 1–2 vs 0 (aOR, 5.42; 95% CI, 1.87–15.75; P = 0.002) were associated with N-overstaging. Among 52 pathologically node-positive patients, N-understaging was less frequent in dMMR than pMMR tumors (11.5% vs 34.6%; P = 0.048), and elevated mGPS was associated with lower odds of N-understaging ( P = 0.030). Conclusions dMMR status, mucinous histology, and elevated mGPS emerged as independent indicators of CT-based N-overstaging in right-sided colon cancer. These tumor- and host-related factors may inform preoperative nodal assessment.

title: A CT-Based and Serum-Derived Nomogram for Preoperative Prediction of Lymphovascular Invasion in Stage Ⅰ Lung Adenocarcinoma
abstract: Abstract Background Lymphovascular invasion (LVI) is a crucial prognostic factor in stage I lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet it can only be confirmed postoperatively. This study aimed to develop a preoperative predictive model for LVI by integrating hematological, clinical, and CT-based radiological features. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 800 patients with stage I LUAD who underwent curative resection. Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression and multivariate logistic regression were employed to identify independent predictors. A nomogram was constructed and internally validated via bootstrap resampling. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results Six independent predictors were identified: neuron-specific enolase (NSE), tumor diameter, consolidation tumor ratio (CTR) > 0.5, spiculation, vacuolar sign, and vessel convergence sign. The nomogram demonstrated good discrimination, with AUCs of 0.841 (95% CI: 0.807–0.875) in the training cohort and 0.786 (95% CI: 0.704–0.868) in the validation cohort. Calibration curves showed excellent agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, and DCA confirmed clinical net benefit across a wide threshold range (5%–80%). Conclusion This simple nomogram incorporating routine CT features and serum NSE offers a robust, noninvasive tool for preoperative individualized prediction of LVI in stage I LUAD, potentially aiding in risk stratification and treatment planning.

title: MESNet: A Lightweight Transformer-CNN Collaborative Network with Morphology Awareness for Glioma Segmentation
abstract: Abstract Glioma segmentation is of great significance for clinical diagnosis and treatment, in which the effective utilization of multimodal information is crucial. Accurate segmentation holds substantial clinical value for guiding precise surgical resection, formulating personalized radiotherapy plans, and assessing prognosis. However, most existing methods focus primarily on the extraction and selection of deep semantic features while overlooking morphologically meaningful features such as edges and shapes. To address this issue, we propose a lightweight high-performance network named MESNet (Morphological Edge and Shape Network). MESNet is a Transformer–CNN collaborative segmentation model that explicitly imposes edge consistency and shape regularity to introduce morphological constraints, thereby enabling precise brain tumor segmentation. The model adopts an efficient 3D Transformer as its backbone, organically integrating convolutional neural networks to capture local details. Through deep complementarity between global context and fine-grained representations, it achieves accurate segmentation. To strengthen boundary awareness, a lightweight multi-scale edge-aware module is designed, which utilizes Sobel-based edge enhancement and spatial attention mechanisms to explicitly sharpen tumor boundaries, substantially reducing boundary errors without significantly increasing computational overhead. To accommodate irregular tumor morphology, an attention-guided shape-aware module is constructed; a zero-initialization strategy is employed to maintain training stability, and the module adaptively focuses on variations in tumor scale and shape, markedly improving the segmentation completeness and contour adherence of small targets such as enhancing tumors. Meanwhile, the network adheres to a lightweight design philosophy, strictly controlling parameter counts and computational complexity through channel compression and efficient attention mechanisms. Experimental results on the BraTS2021 dataset demonstrate that MESNet achieves overall segmentation accuracy and boundary agreement comparable to those of state-of-the-art methods while consuming substantially fewer resources, attaining a superior balance between efficiency and performance. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/tanjia123456/MESNet-main.

title: The Application Value of Ultrasound Soft Markers in the Examination of Common Fetal Chromosomal Aneuploidy Abnormalities: A Retrospective Study
abstract: Abstract Objective To carry out a retrospective cohort study focusing on prevalent soft markers observed in fetal ultrasounds, follow up the incidence of trisomy 21, 18 and 13, and investigate the positive predictive values of single and multiple soft markers for common chromosomal aneuploidy abnormalities. Methods A total of 19,997 pregnant women with ultrasound-detected soft markers underwent non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) or amniocentesis for karyotype analysis and evaluation of chromosomal copy number variations, with their pregnancy outcomes subsequently monitored. The risks of trisomy 21, 18, and 13 associated with various ultrasound soft markers were subjected to statistical analysis. Results A total of 5,530 pregnant women underwent amniocentesis directly, while 14,467 cases received non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), among which 23 high-risk cases proceeded to further amniocentesis. Out of 19,997 fetuses exhibiting ultrasound soft markers, 105 were identified with common chromosomal aneuploidy changes, including 93 cases of trisomy 21, 11 cases of trisomy 18, and 1 case of trisomy 13. The overall positive detection rate was 0.53%. Based on the incidence of common chromosomal aneuploidy abnormalities relative to the risks associated with amniocentesis, the ultrasound soft markers were classified into two categories: high-risk (≥ 0.5%) and low-risk (<0.5%). Isolated ultrasound soft markers were linked to a 0.46% risk of target chromosomal aneuploidy. Among these, thickened nuchal translucency (NT), absence or hypoplasia of the nasal bone, and ventriculomegaly were associated with higher risks of aneuploidy at 4.25%, 2.28%, and 0.98%, respectively. Other markers such as choroid plexus cyst (CPC), single umbilical artery (SUA), aberrant right subclavian artery (ARSA), and echogenic intracardiac focus (EIF) indicated risks of 0.22%, 0.22%, 0.19%, and 0.06%, respectively. No instances of common fetal chromosomal aneuploidy abnormalities were observed in cases with urinary tract dilation, echogenic bowel, or shortened femur length. The overall risk of fetal chromosomal aneuploidy in fetuses with two ultrasound soft markers was 0.92%, including a risk of 0.12% for those with two low-risk markers. When three or more ultrasound soft markers were present, the risk of target chromosomal aneuploidy increased to 4.82%, compared to a 1.6% risk observed in cases with three or more only low-risk soft markers. Conclusions Chromosomal detection strategies can be selected reasonably based on the varying risks of common chromosomal aneuploidy associated with different ultrasound soft markers according to this study. For pregnant women with high‑risk ultrasound soft markers, amniocentesis for prenatal diagnosis is recommended in genetic counseling regardless of the number of soft markers. Amniocentesis is also recommended for those with three or more ultrasound soft markers. For women with one or two low‑risk ultrasound soft markers, NIPT targeting common aneuploidies can be an option under fully informed consent. In this way, medical resources can be reasonably allocated and utilized.

title: The Saturation Gap as a Diagnostic Clue for Methemoglobinemia in a Child with Persistent Low Oxygen Saturation
abstract: Abstract Background Persistent low peripheral oxygen saturation in children commonly prompts investigation for pulmonary or cardiovascular disease. However, when oxygen desaturation persists despite an unrevealing cardiopulmonary evaluation, dyshemoglobinemia should be considered. Case presentation We report the case of a 7-year-old girl with persistent low peripheral oxygen saturation for approximately five years. title: Primary malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor of the vagina: a rare case report
abstract: Abstract Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) is an aggressive sarcoma typically arising from major nerve trunks in the trunk or extremities. Primary MPNST of the vagina is exceptionally rare, with very few cases reported in the literature to date. Herein, we report a rare case of a 67-year-old woman presenting with an 8-month history of vaginal bleeding and fluid discharge. Transvaginal ultrasonography revealed a solid mass (50*40*36 mm) on the posterior vaginal wall. The tumor was completely removed via radical surgical intervention, and the diagnosis of vaginal MPNST was confirmed through pathological examination and immunohistochemical analysis. Although adjuvant radiotherapy was recommended postoperatively based on clinical guidelines, the patient did not undergo this treatment. At the 3-month follow-up, gynecological examination and ultrasonography showed no signs of recurrence. However, one year after surgery, the patient presented with anal pain and discomfort. Pelvic MRI and CT demonstrated extensive recurrent masses in the pelvis and perineum, involving the rectum and anal canal with suspected anal fistula. Systemic evaluation indicated recurrence involving the posterior bladder wall and distal left ureter, resulting in mild left hydronephrosis, along with suspected metastasis to the right hepatic lobe. This case highlights the highly aggressive nature of primary vaginal MPNST and underscores the critical importance of adjuvant therapy and rigorous long-term surveillance for this extremely rare malignancy.

title: Intraoperative Inhalation of Indocyanine Green for Near-Infrared Visualization of Adult Intralobar Pulmonary Sequestration
abstract: Abstract Background The border between sequestered and normal lung in intralobar pulmonary sequestration (ILS) is often indistinct, complicating precise resection. Intravenous indocyanine green (ICG) can outline a perfusion-based boundary but requires prior control of the aberrant systemic artery and does not directly reflect the airway isolation that defines ILS. Case Presentation : Four adults with contrast-enhanced CT-confirmed ILS underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery with intraoperative unilateral ICG inhalation. After single-lung ventilation, aerosolized ICG (2.5 mg/mL) was delivered via a nebulizer connected to the double-lumen tube for 10 to 15 minutes. Near-infrared thoracoscopy showed homogeneous fluorescence in ventilated normal lung and no fluorescence in sequestered tissue, producing a clear demarcation. Three patients underwent wedge resection; one with extensive basal segment involvement underwent lobectomy. No ICG-related adverse events occurred, and all patients recovered uneventfully. Conclusions Intraoperative aerosolized ICG inhalation safely and directly visualizes the ventilation-based boundary characteristic of adult ILS, enabling early lesion mapping and selection of the least extensive complete resection.

title: Edematous dermatomyositis as a rare cause of isolated bilateral arm swelling in a patient with urothelial carcinoma: case report and literature review
abstract: Abstract Background Edematous dermatomyositis (DM) is a rare manifestation of idiopathic inflammatory myopathy and may initially resemble vascular causes of upper-limb swelling. Early recognition is clinically important because severe cases require prompt immunosuppressive treatment and because adult-onset DM, particularly in the presence of anti-transcription intermediary factor 1-gamma (anti-TIF1-γ) antibodies, has a close association with malignancy. Case presentation: An 86-year-old Caucasian woman with recently treated high-grade, muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder presented with a 2.5-week history of progressive, severe bilateral upper-extremity edema, proximal muscle weakness, and a violaceous eruption involving the periorbital region, face, anterior neck, and upper chest, accompanied by Gottron papules. Duplex ultrasonography excluded upper-extremity deep vein thrombosis and superficial venous thrombosis. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography of the chest and abdomen excluded central venous obstruction, thoracic or abdominal tumor recurrence, and metastasis. Electromyography and bilateral shoulder/upper-arm magnetic resonance imaging were compatible with active myositis, and myositis serology was positive for anti-TIF1-γ antibodies. During hospitalization, muscle weakness and dysphagia progressed rapidly. After insufficient clinical response to prednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin, rituximab was administered as salvage therapy. Despite treatment, weakness and dysphagia progressed, and the patient died 6 weeks after admission. Conclusions Edematous dermatomyositis should be considered in the differential diagnosis of otherwise unexplained bilateral upper-limb edema after upper-extremity venous thrombosis and superior vena cava syndrome have been excluded, particularly in the presence of proximal muscle weakness, dysphagia, or dermatomyositis-specific cutaneous findings. The diagnosis of DM should prompt structured oncologic reassessment and surveillance, especially in patients with anti-TIF1-γ positivity or recent malignancy.

title: ATLAS: Development and Evaluation of an AI -Enabled Framework for Anatomically Traceable Measurement Assurance in Fetal-Head Ultrasound Biometry
abstract: Abstract Background Fetal-head biometry is important for estimating gestational age, monitoring fetal development, and identifying abnormalities. As AI-enabled ultrasound systems become more prevalent, automated measurements may appear credible even with mislocalization, suboptimal imaging planes, or absent anatomical landmarks. Clinicians may receive measurements without adequate evidence on their origin or reliability. ATLAS is designed as an evidence-traceable framework to establish conditions for valid measurements. Methods ATLAS consists of a data integrity layer, Find, Confirm, and Measure. The integrity layer performs dataset-agnostic checks for image validity, label consistency, and patient-exclusive partitioning. Find localizes the fetal cranial region; Confirm verifies the anatomical structures required for valid biometry. Measure calculates biparietal diameter, occipitofrontal diameter, and head circumference using two methods: a deterministic localization geometry and a learned segmentation. Training used 3,790 eligible frames from 1,840 patients from public hospital-derived HC18/FETAL_PLANES_DB resources, with patient-exclusive training, validation, and testing; external evaluation used FP (880 frames/460 subjects) and UCL (55/15) cohorts. Outcomes were localization, CSP/LV evidence, and biometric error. Performance measures included availability/IoU, F1, mean absolute error, signed error, and prespecified joint BPD/HC tolerance. Site-specific adaptation and data-free parameter aggregation were added as secondary technical analyses for future edge deployment. Results Under controlled data-fault tests, the data integrity layer detected every introduced defect. Internal validation demonstrated that Find localized all frames (mean IoU 0.962); Confirm F1 was 0.894 for CSP and 0.819 for LV. Deterministic geometry met both biometric tolerances in 91.6% frames versus 84.1% for segmentation, reducing BPD MAE by 0.291 mm (95% CI 0.225–0.355) and improving joint-tolerance performance by 7.5pp (95% CI 5.2–9.9), meaning measurements following positive Confirm being more accurate. Externally, Find localized 99.9% (FP) and 100% (UCL) of frames, with deterministic geometry measurement performing better on FP (91.2%) and segmentation on UCL (79.6%). Site-specific adaptation improved localization but reduced biometry accuracy, which aggregation partially restored. The most memory-intensive ATLAS pathway required 16.50 MB and 57.32 ms per frame. Conclusions This study presents a compact, evidence-traceable framework that treats operationalizing selected ISUOG-relevant anatomical and biometric requirements as computational quality-control states. The system achieves performance comparable to existing approaches, while prioritizing measurement validity and transparency as core design principles. These findings underscore the necessity for clinical AI systems to provide not only accurate results but also interpretable and auditable evidence to support trustworthy integration.

title: Utility of intravoxel incoherent motion diffusion-weighted imaging in predicting pathological response to neoadjuvant immuno-chemotherapy for locally advanced gastric cancer
abstract: Abstract Background To investigate the feasibility of intravoxel incoherent motion diffusion-weighted imaging (IVIM) for predicting pathological tumor regression grade (TRG) after neoadjuvant immuno-chemotherapy (NICT) in locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC). Methods Between January 2022 and December 2024, consecutive patients with endoscopy-biopsy confirmed gastric adenocarcinoma undergoing NICT followed by curative gastrectomy were prospectively recruited. Stomach MRI examinations, including IVIM, were performed within one week before NICT initiation. Patients were classified as responders (TRG 0/1) or non-responders (TRG 2/3). The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), IVIM-derived true diffusion coefficient (D), pseudodiffusion coefficient (D*), and pseudodiffusion fraction ( f ) were measured and compared between the two groups. Independent predictors of non-responders were identified and used to establish a combined parameter. The performances of IVIM-derived parameters were assessed using receiver operating characteristic curve analysis. The relationship between the combined parameter and patient survival outcomes was explored using Kaplan–Meier survival analysis. Results Ninety-three patients (74 males, 19 females; mean age 59.0 ± 9.9 years) were finally recruited. ADC and D were significantly lower, whereas f was higher in non-responders compared with those in responders ( p < 0.05). ADC, D, and f were independent predictors of non-responders. Their combination outperformed each individual parameter, achieving an area under the curve of 0.779, and was associated with patient disease-free survival (DFS) (hazard ratio = 3.624). Conclusion IVIM is feasible for early prediction of treatment response to the emerging NICT in LAGC; ADC, D, and f are equally useful and their combination demonstrated incremental benefit and prognostic value for patient DFS.

title: A Rare Combined Hematoma of the Retzius Space and Broad Ligament Complicating Short Second-Stage Labor: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background Postpartum pelvic hematoma is an uncommon but life-threatening obstetric complication following vaginal delivery. Isolated broad ligament hematomas are occasionally reported, while hematomas confined to the Retzius space are extremely rare. Concurrent composite hematoma involving both anatomical compartments after short second-stage labor represents a scarcely reported clinical entity. This concealed hemorrhagic condition presents with non-specific symptoms, often leading to delayed diagnosis and increased maternal morbidity. Case presentation : A 33-year-old gravida 2, para 1 woman achieved vaginal delivery at 38 weeks of gestation with a short second-stage labor of 27 minutes. Three hours postpartum, the patient developed persistent suprapubic pain and urinary retention without remarkable external vaginal bleeding. Physical examination revealed hypotension, suprapubic tenderness, and tense anterior vaginal fornix. Laboratory tests showed a marked hemoglobin decline from 116 g/L to 85 g/L. Pelvic ultrasound identified a large 14.4 × 9.2 × 9.0 cm Retzius space hematoma. Considering progressive anemia and hemodynamic instability, emergency exploratory laparotomy was performed. Intraoperative findings confirmed synchronous hematomas in the Retzius space and right broad ligament. A bleeding point beneath the infundibulopelvic ligament was identified and ligated. The broad ligament peritoneum was closed with interrupted sutures. The patient had an uneventful postoperative course and was discharged on postoperative day 5. Conclusions Combined Retzius space and broad ligament hematoma is a rare concealed postpartum emergency strongly associated with precipitous labor. Atypical urinary symptoms without obvious vaginal bleeding easily led to misdiagnosis. Venous-origin diffuse bleeding limits the efficacy of arterial embolization. For large multi-compartment hematomas with compressive symptoms, open laparotomy enables thorough hemostasis and resolves pelvic mass effects effectively. Early clinical suspicion and timely surgical intervention are critical for favorable maternal outcomes.

title: Cost-effectiveness of Active Screening Strategies for Detecting Asymptomatic Tuberculosis in China: A Markov Model
abstract: Abstract Objective This study evaluated the costs and cost-effectiveness of active case-finding strategies for detecting asymptomatic tuberculosis among close contacts of active tuberculosis patients in China using a Markov model, with the aim of informing the optimization of tuberculosis screening strategies. Methods A decision tree combined with a Markov model was developed from the healthcare system perspective to compare four screening strategies among close contacts of active tuberculosis patients: passive case finding, chest radiography with human interpretation, chest radiography assisted by computer-aided detection, and pooled GeneXpert testing. A hypothetical cohort was simulated over a 20-year time horizon. The primary outcome was the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER), expressed as cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained. Strategies were evaluated against China’s willingness-to-pay (WTP) threshold of ¥298,995 per quality-adjusted life year. Results Active case-finding strategies reduced tuberculosis cases and deaths compared with passive case finding.. Pooled GeneXpert testing produced the greatest health benefit, reducing surviving tuberculosis cases by 3,738 and cumulative deaths by 812 per 100,000 close contacts compared with passive case finding. Compared with chest radiography assisted by computer-aided detection, pooled GeneXpert testing achieved an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of ¥1,117.40 per quality-adjusted life year gained, well below the willingness-to-pay threshold. Conclusion Pooled GeneXpert testing was the most cost-effective strategy for detecting asymptomatic tuberculosis among close contacts in China, while computer-aided chest radiography may serve as a low-cost alternative in resource-limited settings.

title: Equity-aware stochastic optimization of mammography screening facility location under demand and capacity uncertainty
abstract: Abstract Uneven geographic access to mammography can limit participation in breast cancer screening, particularly in rural and underserved communities. We developed a statewide planning framework that combines geospatial accessibility analysis with stochastic facility-location optimization to identify locations for new mammography facilities under uncertainty in screening demand and existing-facility capacity. The analysis included 5.58 million Texas women aged 40–74 years, 615 existing facilities, and 222 candidate locations. The model first maximized expected screening coverage and then reduced population-weighted differences in potential access across eight race and ethnicity groups without sacrificing coverage. Opening 62 facilities across 58 counties increased expected coverage from 92.47% to 98.09% and reduced expected unmet demand from 420,089 to 106,822 women annually. Between-group variance (BGV) in access decreased by 32%, while access for the worst-served group increased from 0.858 to 0.953 effective screening slots per eligible woman. All selected locations were in baseline access-gap areas; 44% were in nonmetropolitan counties and 39% established the first mammography facility in their county. Explicitly modeling uncertainty reduced expected unmet demand by 29,643 women compared with deterministic planning. These results show that a modest, equity-aware expansion of fixed mammography capacity can substantially widen screening access and narrow both racial and geographic disparities—by placing facilities where under-served populations live rather than where volume is highest—while the most remote communities are better served by mobile screening than by additional fixed sites.

title: Radiomics-Based Muscle Quality Assessment from Multi-Site Multi-Vendor MRI
abstract: Abstract Muscle strength is critical for mobility, and its decline with aging contributes to frailty, falls, and loss of independence. Muscle cross-sectional area (CSA), which can be measured on MRI, only reflects muscle quantity and may not fully capture age-related changes in muscle composition, which significantly contribute to loss of muscle strength in older adults. We investigated strength prediction using multi-center/multi-scanner Dixon MRI from 141 adults across three cohorts: 82 healthy adults (Philips, 22–94 years), 24 healthy adults (GE, 30–79 years), and 35 older adults (Siemens, 70–91 years), including healthy, pre-frail, and sarcopenic participants. CSA was a strong predictor of muscle strength in the healthy cohorts, but radiomics features provided additional value when older adults were included. Fat-fraction radiomics showed the strongest and most consistent performance across cohort combinations, with the best results in the full combined cohort (R²=0.64 versus 0.42 for CSA alone). Water-only radiomics also retained predictive value, although generally less strongly than fat-fraction features. The most informative radiomics features reflected muscle size, signal magnitude, and internal heterogeneity, and SHAP analysis linked higher intramuscular heterogeneity to reduced strength. Taken together, these findings suggest that radiomics can capture muscle quality features that affect muscle force-generating capacity beyond size alone, particularly in older adults, and support automated MRI-based assessment of muscle composition and function, which potentially help future sarcopenia screening and functional risk stratification.

The most informative radiomics features reflected muscle size, signal magnitude, and internal heterogeneity, and SHAP analysis linked higher intramuscular heterogeneity to reduced strength. Taken together, these findings suggest that radiomics can capture muscle quality features that affect muscle force-generating capacity beyond size alone, particularly in older adults, and support automated MRI-based assessment of muscle composition and function, which potentially help future sarcopenia screening and functional risk stratification.

title: Pseudoangina as an Unusual Presentation of Non-Osseous Arterial Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: A Case Report.
abstract: Abstract Background Thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) encompasses disorders caused by compression of the neurovascular structures traversing the thoracic outlet. Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome (aTOS) is the rarest subtype, accounting for approximately 1% of cases. It is typically associated with cervical ribs or other osseous abnormalities and carries a significant risk of distal embolization and limb-threatening ischemia. Presentation with recurrent angina-like chest pain is uncommon and may result in diagnostic delay. Case Presentation A 27-year-old previously healthy man presented with recurrent left-sided chest pain radiating to the neck and left upper limb for four weeks. Initial investigations for a cardiac cause, including serial electrocardiograms, cardiac biomarkers, transthoracic echocardiography, treadmill stress testing, coronary angiography, and Holter monitoring, were normal. Further evaluation revealed intermittent left upper-limb paresthesia and cold intolerance. The Adson maneuver reproduced symptoms and was associated with attenuation of the left radial pulse and dusky discoloration of the fingers. Chest and cervical spine radiographs showed no cervical rib or other osseous abnormality. Dynamic computed tomography angiography demonstrated positional compression of the left subclavian artery during arm abduction, which resolved in the neutral position, while dynamic venography was normal. A diagnosis of left-sided non-osseous arterial thoracic outlet syndrome was established. The patient was referred for vascular surgical evaluation and thoracic outlet decompression. Conclusion Arterial thoracic outlet syndrome should be considered in young patients with recurrent non-cardiac chest pain, particularly when accompanied by upper-limb neurovascular symptoms. A high index of suspicion and dynamic vascular imaging are critical for timely diagnosis, especially in the absence of the osseous abnormalities classically associated with aTOS.

title: Prevalence of Diabetic Retinopathy in Children Aged ≥10 Years with Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus Attending the Diabetic Clinic at Kassala Teaching Hospital, Sudan: A Cross-Sectional Study, August–December 2025
abstract: Abstract Background : Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a leading microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus and a major cause of preventable visual impairment. Although traditionally considered an adult disease, DR is increasingly recognized among children and adolescents with diabetes. Early detection and management are essential to prevent irreversible vision loss. However, in Sudan, limited data exist on the prevalence and risk factors of DR among pediatric diabetic patients. Method: A descriptive, cross-sectional, hospital-based study was conducted at the Diabetic Clinic of Kassala Teaching Hospital from August to December 2025. The study included 115 children aged over ten years diagnosed with type 1 diabetes. Data were collected using a structured, interview-administered questionnaire and clinical examination, including fundus evaluation. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS version 26 to assess frequencies and associations between diabetic retinopathy and relevant demographic and clinical factors. Result: The study included 115 participants, of whom 60.9% were females and 39.1% were males. The prevalence of diabetic retinopathy was 1.7%, with two cases identified: one mild non-proliferative DR and one moderate non-proliferative DR with clinically significant macular edema. Poor glycemic control was common, with 51.3% of participants having HbA1c levels above 10%. Most participants (96.5%) had never undergone previous eye screening. No statistically significant associations were found between diabetic retinopathy and glycemic control (p = 1.000), duration of diabetes (p = 0.534), age group (p = 0.119), or gender (p = 1.000). However, the very small number of DR cases substantially limited the statistical power to detect associations. Conclusion: The prevalence of DR in our study was low (1.7%). Nevertheless, DR was identified in two children, including one with severe NPDR and DME. The high frequency of suboptimal glycemic control and the very low uptake of previous retinal screening highlight important gaps in pediatric diabetes eye care. Larger prospective studies are needed to better characterize the burden and risk factors of DR among children with diabetes in Sudan.

title: Reproducibility-Aware Evaluation of Hierarchical Multiple- Instance Learning for Patient-Level Thrombosis Detection from Compression Ultrasound
abstract: Abstract Background To provide a reproducibility-aware evaluation of multi-site cine multiple-instance learning (MS-CineMIL) versus a fixed 8-frame imaging baseline under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, and to examine whether the nominal ROC AUC difference reproduces after field completion and runtime environment control. The study delineates aggregation applicability boundaries rather than presupposing a stable advantage. Methods The public ThrombUS+ Dataset #1 Training Set (v1.0; 594 subjects, 2,341 DICOM cine clips) was used. Thrombosis is a per-site label, so the patient-level endpoint was defined as engineering-positive: raw Thrombosis = 1 for any record of the same SubjectID (81/594). After quality control, 2,327 cines were retained. Partitions used SubjectID isolation. Primary metric: ROC AUC; secondary: PR AUC, Brier score. Model differences were tested by 10,000-resample patient-level paired bootstrap (empirical two-sided P values; Bonferroni α = 0.0167). Results In the V1 historical frozen analysis, the ROC AUC difference of MS-CineMIL versus the fixed 8-frame baseline was + 0.0740 (95% CI 0.0043 to 0.1454, P = 0.039), failing Bonferroni correction. In the same-environment controlled comparison, the difference was − 0.0283 (95% CI − 0.1177 to 0.0608, P = 0.538) with a larger Brier error (+ 0.0374, P < 0.001). The baseline re-run yielded 0.6390; the complete model ROC AUC was 0.6419. The between-run baseline shift (0.0711) matched the nominal gain (+ 0.0740); no stable advantage emerged. Conclusions The V1 frozen difference did not pass multiple-comparison correction, was not reproduced under controlled comparison, and was accompanied by a larger Brier error. Evidence supports boundary auditing of model components, field completeness, and aggregation strategies, but not stable superiority, clinical deployment, external applicability, or novelty claims.

title: Clinically Suspected Systemic Arterial Gas Embolism during Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy: a Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Systemic arterial gas embolism (SAGE) is a rare but potentially catastrophic complication of robotic-assisted bronchoscopy with lung biopsy. During general anesthesia, the earliest manifestations of SAGE may be limited to transient electrocardiographic or hemodynamic abnormalities. The absence of visible intracranial gas on subsequent imaging does not exclude the diagnosis. We report a case of clinically suspected SAGE during robotic-assisted bronchoscopy in which intraoperative sentinel signs preceded delayed emergence and focal neurologic injury. Case presentation: A 78-year-old woman underwent robotic-assisted bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for biopsy of a 4.6-cm right middle lobe ground-glass opacity using transbronchial needle aspiration and cryobiopsy. Significant airway bleeding occurred after sampling. Immediately after biopsy, she developed transient tachycardia, hypertension, bradycardia, and ST-segment elevation in lead V5. Although these abnormalities resolved, she was unresponsive shortly after extubation and developed right gaze deviation, facial twitching, abnormal movements, and absent right upper-extremity withdrawal to pain. Head computed tomography showed no acute abnormality, and brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated left frontal and precentral cortical diffusion restriction without visible intracranial gas. Because SAGE was strongly suspected, she received 100% oxygen, levetiracetam, endotracheal reintubation, and hyperbaric oxygen therapy at 2.8 atmospheres absolute approximately 4 hours after bronchoscopy. High-sensitivity troponin I peaked at 5,116 ng/L and left ventricular ejection fraction improved from 45-50% to 60% the following day. She was extubated on post-procedure day 10 with persistent neurologic deficits. On post-procedure day 18, she experienced hypoxic cardiac arrest associated with bilateral pulmonary emboli and an acute aortic dissection and died the following day after transition to comfort-focused care. Conclusions: During bronchoscopic biopsies under general anesthesia, unexplained ST-segment changes, hemodynamic instability, or delayed neurologic recovery should prompt immediate consideration of SAGE, even when initial neuroimaging is negative. Administration of 100% oxygen, airway and hemodynamic support, minimization of airway pressures, and urgent consultation for hyperbaric oxygen therapy should not be delayed while awaiting radiographic confirmation.

title: Adenosquamous carcinoma of the colon with an aberrant MLH1 immunostaining pattern: a diagnostic pitfall in mismatch repair assessment
abstract: Abstract Background Adenosquamous carcinoma (ASC) is a rare histological subtype of colorectal cancer (CRC) that carries a poor prognosis and has been associated with a distinct molecular profile - higher frequency of mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR), PD-L1 overexpression, and KRAS mutations. With recent advances in CRC therapeutics, molecular characterization of rare histological subtypes has become increasingly important. Here, we report a case of colorectal ASC with a distinctive dMMR immunohistochemical profile and provide a review of the literature on this rare colorectal neoplasm. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 64-year-old woman who presented with a three-month history of worsening abdominal pain and recent-onset hematochezia. Abdominal CT revealed a large mass involving the right colon. She underwent a total pelvic exenteration. Histopathology showed a high-grade, poorly differentiated tumor with mixed glandular and squamous components, staged as pT4b pN1a. Immunohistochemistry confirmed both glandular and squamous differentiation. Mismatch repair protein analysis showed loss of PMS2 expression and a granular, dot-like MLH1 staining pattern—interpreted as loss of expression and consistent with a known clone-specific artifact—while MSH2 and MSH6 were retained, supporting a dMMR phenotype. The patient received mFLOX chemotherapy but died four months postoperatively due to disease-related complications. Discussion This case illustrates the classic clinicopathological features of ASC, alongside a dMMR immunoprofile that may carry therapeutic relevance given the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in MSI-high colorectal tumors. The findings also underscore the importance of correctly recognizing clone-specific MLH1 staining artifacts, as misinterpretation could falsely suggest isolated PMS2 loss and trigger unnecessary germline testing for Lynch syndrome. Given the rarity of ASC and its limited molecular characterization, accurate MMR status assessment remains critical for guiding treatment decisions and avoiding diagnostic pitfalls.

title: A generalized similarity metric based on Sobolev space geometry for deformable image registration in image-guided radiotherapy
abstract: Abstract Background : Deformable image registration is an essential technique in image-guided adaptive radiotherapy. It provides voxelwise estimates of the anatomical deformations from medical image volumes acquired at different time points. However, the accuracy of the estimated motion strongly depends on image contrast, presence of noise and artifacts, and the overall image quality. Purpose : This study introduces a novel similarity metric based on the geometry of Sobolev spaces. The proposed metric provides control over the contribution of high-order image features, allowing the metric to adapt to the characteristics of the images. It unifies several established similarity metrics and enables efficient numerical computation for integration into existing registration methods. Methods : The metric was integrated into a deformable image registration algorithm and evaluated on three experiments relevant for adaptive radiotherapy: thoracic and abdominal CT registration and pre- to post-operative brain MR image registration. Registration accuracy was assessed using alignment of anatomical landmarks. Results : The proposed similarity metric achieved rapid and accurate image alignment in all three scenarios. Increasing the contribution from higher-order image features improved the estimated deformation fields by a reduction of the landmark error. In particular, increased weighting of these features improved the alignment of liver vessels and the brain cavity following tumor resection. Conclusions : The proposed metric provides the flexibility to control the relative contribution of image features for deformable image registration. It unifies several established similarity metrics while maintaining computational efficiency and accuracy standards that are compatible with image-guided radiotherapy.

title: Interactive Lesion Segmentation in Whole-Body PET/CT and Longitudinal CT: The autoPET/CT-IV Challenge
abstract: Abstract Deep learning enables automated tumour segmentation in whole-body positron emission tomography and computed tomography, but robustness remains limited by heterogeneous tracer uptake, anatomical variability, and inter-center differences. We report the fourth autoPET challenge, which evaluated interactive lesion segmentation using incremental simulated user prompts and longitudinal lesion segmentation from paired baseline and follow-up scans. In the interactive task (Task 1, ~ 30,000 training and ~ 3,000 test lesions), submitted methods improved with additional user input and achieved a mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.74 at the final interaction step, with performance remaining robust across tracers and centers. Longitudinal segmentation (Task 2, ~ 7,500 training and ~ 4,500 test lesions) was substantially more challenging, with a best mean Dice similarity coefficient of 0.38. Here, we show that interactive segmentation can combine automated inference with iterative expert input while maintaining performance across heterogeneous imaging domains, whereas longitudinal lesion prediction remains limited by temporal and anatomical variability.

title: Halo-Femoral Traction and Staged Surgical Correction for Severe Rigid Adult Scoliosis: A Case Report
abstract: Abstract Background: Surgical correction of severe rigid adult spinal deformities (ASD) with Cobb angles exceeding 100° is highly challenging due to risks of neurological injury and poor spinal flexibility. Preoperative halo-femoral traction enhances spinal compliance, facilitating safer staged corrective surgery. Few cases of this procedure for curvatures approaching 150° have been reported. Case Presentation: A 24-year-old female presented with severe right thigh and knee pain secondary to a 148° rigid thoracolumbar kyphoscoliosis. Initial imaging revealed minimal flexibility (bend correction to 94°) without neural compromise. The patient underwent continuous halo-femoral traction for several weeks to improve spinal flexibility, The patient was managed via a sequential two-step protocol: initially, under anesthesia, halo and femoral pins were placed to apply continuous traction for maximizing spinal flexibility. Subsequently, the patient underwent definitive single-stage posterior spinal instrumentation and deformity correction. Intraoperative neuromonitoring was utilized throughout to ensure neurological safety. Continuous multi-modal intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM), including somatosensory-evoked potentials (SSEPs) and motor-evoked potentials (MEPs), was utilized throughout all two surgical stages. No significant or sustained changes in SSEP or MEP signals were observed during the corrective maneuvers, supporting the early detection of potential neurological compromise and guiding safe deformity correction. Conclusion: Postoperatively, the patient achieved significant correction with a final Cobb angle of approximately 50°, accompanied by marked pain relief, improved truncal balance, and enhanced functional status as measured by clinical video-based clinical observation of gait. Radiographs at 6 weeks and subsequent follow-ups demonstrated stable fusion and sustained alignment. No neurological deficits or major complications were observed. This case illustrates the feasibility of utilizing prolonged halo-femoral traction combined with a carefully planned surgical algorithm in the management of extreme rigid adult scoliosis. The technical and strategic framework provided herein may inform clinical practice guidelines and warrants further investigation in larger cohorts.

title: Assistance curve analysis: evaluating the clinical value of AI-assisted decision making
abstract: Abstract Background. Clinical AI is almost never used alone. It shows something to a doctor, and the doctor decides. Yet the measures used to judge them describe the model, not the decision. A 2025 overview of 32 performance measures for clinical AI covers five domains, and current standard metrics do not explicitly evaluate the decisions of an assisted clinician in a paired setting. Methods. We define the net benefit of assistance, ΔNB(p), as the difference in net benefit between the decisions a clinician makes with an AI available and those they make without it. We show that ΔNB depends only on cases where the clinician changed their mind, and give a closed form in four quantities: how often the AI moves the clinician each way, and how often it is right when it does. This yields a break-even rule, a number needed to consult, and an override profile. We checked the estimators by simulation and applied the method to Collab-CXR, a public study of 227 radiologists reading chest X-rays with and without a CheXpert-trained model. Results. ΔNB(p) = [r U (π U − p) + r L (p − π L )]/(1 − p). Across 27,720 paired decisions by 33 radiologists, the AI made them less accurate by 0.83 percentage points while making their decisions better. ΔNB was + 0.0022 at p = 0.05 (95% CI + 0.0007 to + 0.0038), a 7% gain on the unaided radiologist’s net benefit, or one extra net true positive per 455 decisions. The benefit was clear between thresholds of 0.02 and 0.05; above 0.05 the interval included zero, and below about 0.019 both arms were beaten by acting on every finding. The break-even threshold was 0.201. Two further designs covering 194 radiologists agreed in direction. Effects ranged from + 0.0131 for atelectasis to − 0.0024 for cardiomediastinal abnormality. Conclusions. The value of an AI is made on the decisions it changes and cannot be read off accuracy. Judging by accuracy would have rejected a tool that improved decisions. The method needs only what a paired reader study already collects, and free software is provided for R and Python.

We show that ΔNB depends only on cases where the clinician changed their mind, and give a closed form in four quantities: how often the AI moves the clinician each way, and how often it is right when it does. This yields a break-even rule, a number needed to consult, and an override profile. We checked the estimators by simulation and applied the method to Collab-CXR, a public study of 227 radiologists reading chest X-rays with and without a CheXpert-trained model. Results. ΔNB(p) = [r U (π U  − p) + r L (p − π L )]/(1 − p). Across 27,720 paired decisions by 33 radiologists, the AI made them less accurate by 0.83 percentage points while making their decisions better. ΔNB was + 0.0022 at p = 0.05 (95% CI + 0.0007 to + 0.0038), a 7% gain on the unaided radiologist’s net benefit, or one extra net true positive per 455 decisions. The benefit was clear between thresholds of 0.02 and 0.05; above 0.05 the interval included zero, and below about 0.019 both arms were beaten by acting on every finding. The break-even threshold was 0.201. Two further designs covering 194 radiologists agreed in direction. Effects ranged from + 0.0131 for atelectasis to − 0.0024 for cardiomediastinal abnormality. Conclusions. The value of an AI is made on the decisions it changes and cannot be read off accuracy. Judging by accuracy would have rejected a tool that improved decisions.
